attack.final_span:
— feels sluggish through quick transitions, to the point you’ll want to SLS it if you’re a keen driver.
On the open road, the Stelvio presents as a magnificent sight, marked by its oddly puffed-up rear windscreen resembling a quirky rabbit-ears design; press the key fob, and the screen magically adjusts, much like a playful Cheshire cat.
Remember not to press the button too quickly — the penny-fed, flip-screen tailgate descends harshly onto the bumper, almost tipping over your full grocery haul, child, or even two small bear-sized objects.
Old Italian hands recall the Stelvio had differing guises over the years, both for road and track. This one wears Stelvio on the bonnet, which suggests the car is porpoising off the road, not on it. The legend is the name refers to the guy who corresponds and is the point of contact at Alfa headquarters. I wouldn’t know.
Looking really good in both Aurum (more yellow than orange) and Sprint (more orange than yellow). Armoured spec offers minimal bling but effective styling upgrades.
The $1500 GQ edition stands out for its distinct value, featuring a matte finish in a prominent gray shade, rather than the fake piano black lacquer.
A sharp and sporty ride, along with capable handling, courtesy of its double wishbone MacPherson strut front and multilink rear suspensions. More suitable than Dinamica to hold its all-important damping.
Proper Italian leather seats and lovely carpet. Wi-Fi, air conditioning, heated seats, and smartphone mirroring are standard features, with luxury enhancements available in the Requirement, 85 Pack, Traveller, or Assist Speciale configurations.
More Stuttgart than Milano on the specsheet; reasonably refined noise and vibration; appetite for premium fuel. Quadrifoglio bit, properly made of course, sounds like a devilish thing.
